html:
The Trans-Siberian Railway is the line that links Moscow with Vladivostok on the Pacific, built by the Russian Empire between 1891 and 1916. At over 9,000 kilometres it is the longest railway line in the world.

Russia had held Siberia since the conquest of the 1500s and 1600s, but reaching it meant months by river and cart. Emperor Alexander III ordered the railway, and his son Nicholas II, as heir, laid the first stone at Vladivostok in 1891. The finance minister Sergei Witte drove the project.

Building it was hard:

  • It crossed permafrost, great rivers and the mountains around Lake Baikal. For a time trains crossed the lake on ferries, and in winter on rails laid over the ice.
  • To save time, an early route cut across Manchuria as the Chinese Eastern Railway, which drew Russia into Chinese affairs.
  • The line was single track at first and could not carry enough troops in the Russo-Japanese War of 1904 to 1905.
  • The all-Russian route along the Amur was finished in 1916.

The railway changed Siberia. Millions of peasants moved east to farm, and grain, timber and later minerals moved west. It made Russia a Pacific power and tied Siberia to Europe. Later lines such as the Turksib Railway linked it to Central Asia.
sum: The Trans-Siberian Railway is the line that links Moscow with Vladivostok on the Pacific, built by the Russian Empire between 1891 and 1916. At over 9,000 kilometres it is the longest railway line in the world.
